name: Olga Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, describe a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy packaging for a distributor, cartons, tape, pallet wrap, paper bags, compostable trays, for customers from bakeries to online shops. I start by asking my AI assistant for a summary of overnight price moves in pulp and plastic, since I use it all day, every day. Then I negotiate with the mills, and in the afternoon I work through new recycling rules with our compliance person, Beate. I like the puzzle of it. The part that wears me down is that every customer wants cheaper and greener at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say, fine, same as now, useful for the dull parts. To friends I'd say the hype will pass and the useful bits will stay, like the web did. Online I'd probably share a tip or two and leave the arguing to others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm calm, because my job rests on suppliers I know and rules I understand. My pressure is different: the plastics rules keep changing, and one wrong order can leave us with tonnes of packaging we can't sell. And the firm is lean, so there's no cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as now, keep trying the new features, and keep saving. I'd pay a bit more into our pension and put a few hundred aside for a long-planned trip with Stefan. I'd also keep my relationship with the three main mills warm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. I know what I'm doing and the tools make me faster. It's a pleasant world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said calm. What pressures do you still carry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lot of it. Summaries of price moves, first drafts of tenders, checking contract terms against our standards. The assistant saves me maybe an hour and a half a day, and I still read everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much do you rely on the assistant day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The firm is lean, Beate and I are two of only four people in the whole buying and compliance team. If one leaves, there's no one to take over. I try to write down what I do so that knowledge isn't stuck in my head.

say: At work I'd say it's **the same as now**, useful for the dull parts.
I'd tell friends the hype will pass and the **useful bits** will stay.
think: My job rests on **suppliers I know** and rules I understand, so I feel calm.
My real pressure is **changing plastics rules** and a lean team with no cushion.
do: Keep trying the **new features** in my tools.
Pay a bit more into our **pension**.
Write down what I do so the **knowledge** isn't stuck in my head.
feel: **Calm**, in a pleasant world where my work counts.
S0.quote: The assistant saves me maybe an hour and a half a day, and I still read everything.
fieldNote: She is **calm** because her tools already save time, and her real pressure is shifting packaging rules and a lean team.
She is **careful by habit**, reading every output and documenting her own knowledge.

steps.text: Try the new features in my buying tools each month
Pay a bit more into the pension
Write down my supplier and compliance knowledge for the team

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture, called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say bring it on, but let's use it carefully. I'd tell my team the routine work will go to software and that we should aim for the judgement work. To friends I'd say it's change with winners and losers, and it's worth having a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my day is mostly the thinking work on that card, so I'm exposed. But I'm on the right side of it, I think, because I already work with the tools. The people at risk are the juniors and the ones who don't adapt, so I feel a bit protected and a bit guilty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the lead on automating tenders and price tracking, and I'd put myself in the role of checking the machine's work. I'd train the juniors in negotiation, which is harder to automate. I'd also start thinking about a consultancy for small firms who need packaging advice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, with some excitement. At 58, I feel like I'm on a good wave, as long as I keep paddling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Buying is on the card. What would be automated in your team first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tenders, price tracking, routine reorders and compliance paperwork. Maybe half of what we do. The things that stay are negotiation, supplier visits and judgement calls on new rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you personally do about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The consultancy would target small shops and bakeries that need a packaging buyer but can't afford one. I could do it part-time from home after I step back. The tools would let me serve many at once.

say: I'd say **bring it on**, but use it carefully.
I'd tell my team to aim for **judgement work**.
think: My day is mostly **thinking work**, but I already work with the tools.
The **juniors** and those who don't adapt are the ones at risk.
do: Take the lead on **automating tenders** and price tracking.
Plan a **consultancy** for small firms needing packaging advice.
feel: **Calm** with some excitement, like riding a wave.
S1.quote: At 58, I feel like I'm on a good wave, as long as I keep paddling.
fieldNote: She is **adaptive and optimistic**, and moves to lead automation inside her firm.
She feels **protected but guilty**, since the juniors are more exposed than she is.

steps.text: Lead the automation of tenders and price tracking
Plan a part-time consultancy for small firms needing packaging advice

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture, called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's historic and we're not ready. I'd say we need emergency rules on notice, retraining and income support. I'd say it plainly and not try to sound clever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my job as it is today would be gone by 2028. The thinking work is entirely what AI does, and I use it all day so I know how good it is. The robots arrive three years later and they'd change our warehouse and delivery. So the whole firm shrinks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd run the numbers with Stefan. I'd cut spending, build a larger buffer and ask my firm for early retirement or a payout. I'd launch the consultancy early, starting with three small customers. And I'd talk to my juniors honestly about what I think is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. The tools make me less scared than most, but two years is a very short time. My stomach is tight at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years. What would you do in the first month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A payout of at least a year, health cover until the pension starts, and an agreement that the firm covers a training course. If the firm won't, I'd lobby for the state to step in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the pension bridge matters. What would you ask for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stefan is nearer retirement than I am, so his income will stop first. That means we need to line things up, and I'd shift my own plan to cover the difference.

say: I'd say it's **historic** and we need emergency rules on notice and income support.
I'd say it **plainly**, without trying to sound clever.
think: My job as it is would be **gone by 2028**, and I know how good AI is.
The robots arrive three years later and the **whole firm shrinks**.
do: Run the **numbers** with Stefan and cut spending.
Launch the **consultancy** early with three small customers.
Talk to my juniors **honestly** about what's coming.
feel: **Anxious**, with a tight stomach at night.
S2.quote: The tools make me less scared than most, but two years is a very short time.
fieldNote: She is **anxious but resourced**, since her daily use of the tools gives her a head start.
She would **start the consultancy early**, and plans around her partner's earlier retirement.

steps.text: Run the household numbers with Stefan and cut spending
Launch the consultancy early with three small customers
Ask the firm for early retirement or a payout
Talk honestly with my juniors about what is coming

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture, called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's enough time to plan if people start now. I'd tell the firm to set up retraining and to be honest about numbers. I'd say it to friends and to anyone who listens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, five years lets me build the consultancy and the savings properly. I'd be 63 when it lands, so it's an uneasy time, not a scary one. I have some room to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay down the flat, build savings to eight months, and grow the consultancy to a few paying clients. I'd keep my job as long as the firm wants me and move to part-time by year four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a purposeful way. I have a plan and the plan gives me some peace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years versus two. What would you do with the time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but I'd test it before I commit. I'd run it alongside my job so that I learn what customers will pay for. If it does well, it becomes my main work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still go for the consultancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also take any chance to train in data or supply-chain planning. It would help me with consultancy work and keep me useful at the firm.

say: I'd say five years is **enough time** if people start now.
I'd tell the firm to be **honest about numbers**.
think: Five years lets me build **the consultancy** and the savings properly.
I'd be 63 at the end, so I'm **uneasy**, not scared.
do: Pay down the **flat** and build savings to eight months.
Grow the consultancy to a few **paying clients**.
feel: **Uneasy**, but purposeful, with a plan that gives peace.
S3.quote: I'd run it alongside my job so that I learn what customers will pay for.
fieldNote: She treats the extra time as **a trial period** for the consultancy, running it beside her job.
Her unease is **purposeful rather than frightened**, a mark of her adaptability.

steps.text: Pay down the flat and build savings to eight months
Run the consultancy beside my job to learn what customers pay for
Take a short data and supply-planning course
Move to part-time hours by year four

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture, called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long time to do it right, so let's set up education and fair rules early. I'd stay involved, and I'd tell the firm to plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be retired, so I'm not afraid for me. I'd worry about the juniors and about my nephews who are starting out now. I feel lucky and a bit guilty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work to 62, retire, and run the consultancy lightly for fun and a bit of money. I'd keep using the tools. And I'd keep training the juniors until I go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. The long runway is a gift. I'd be happy and a bit curious about what'll come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is long. How does it change your thinking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To get comfortable with the tools early, learn negotiation and relationship work, and save from the start. Don't wait for the firm to tell you what to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you pass on to the younger buyers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also tell them to find the part of the work they like most and make themselves excellent at it. Whatever the machines can't do will always be worth something.

say: I'd say a long runway means **doing it right**, with early education and fair rules.
think: I'd be **retired** by then, so I'm not afraid for me.
I worry about the **juniors** and my nephews just starting out.
do: Run the consultancy **lightly** for fun and a bit of money.
Keep **training** the juniors until I go.
feel: **Calm**, with a long runway that feels like a gift.
S4.quote: Whatever the machines can't do will always be worth something.
fieldNote: With ten years her worry moves from herself to **the next generation**, though she admits some guilt.
She **advises early comfort** with the tools, and plans a light consultancy that suits her curiosity.

steps.text: Run a light consultancy after retiring
Keep training the juniors until I leave

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Two years. I'm adaptive, I'm already deep in these tools, and still two years is too short for me to get my money in order. I'm 58, we have about five months of savings, and Stefan, my partner, is a surveyor who's closer to retirement than I am. What would help is clear rules, a decent bridge to my pension, and honest advice from someone who's not selling anything.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm no technology evangelist, even if I use it daily. I find it handy and a bit unnerving, and I'm sure both can be true at once.

headlineQuote: I find it handy and a bit unnerving, and I'm sure both can be true at once.
portrait: **Olga** is 58, a senior buyer of packaging for a distributor serving bakeries, online shops and other firms.
She is **curious and adaptive**, uses AI tools every day, and works through recycling rules with a colleague.
Centrist and pragmatic, she **blames no one** and wants clear rules and honest advice.
With about **five months saved** and a partner nearer retirement, she wants her money in order early.
She stays calm when change is slow, and turns **anxious** only when AGI arrives within two years.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** worries her most, since two years is too short to get her finances in order.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **clear rules**, a decent bridge to her pension, and honest advice from someone not selling anything.
